sources.title: Peter Webb, A Course in Finite Group Representation Theory
sources.locator: Printed contents pp. iv-v; Chapter 1 §§1.1-1.2, pp. 1-10; Chapter 2 §2.1 and Exercise 12, pp. 14-26; Chapter 4 Proposition 4.2.1, Example 4.2.2, and the opening of §4.3 including Propositions 4.3.1-4.3.2 and Example 4.3.4, pp. 53-58; Chapter 6 §6.3 and Exercises 13, 15, 21-22, pp. 89-107; Chapter 9 §§9.1-9.2, pp. 141-145.

contents.name: Example 1.1.3 the standard real representation of S_3
Example 1.1.4 the nonsplit C_p representation in characteristic p
contents.reason: This example is the canonical counterexample to Maschke's theorem and to invariant complements. The design explicitly homes that failure on RT-2 rather than planting it on the introductory dictionary page.

contents.name: Example 1.1.6 a direct-sum representation of C_2
Example 1.1.7 a subrepresentation that is not a direct summand
contents.reason: This is Webb's explicit failure-of-complements witness, so it belongs with Maschke's theorem on RT-2 rather than with the introductory definitions and dictionary on RT-1.

contents.name: Theorem 1.2.1 (Maschke)
contents.reason: Complete reducibility is the landmark of the next page, where the averaging proof, the characteristic hypothesis, and the semisimple-module consequences all belong together.

contents.name: Lemma 1.2.3 splitting submodules out of a sum of simples
contents.reason: This lemma is internal semisimple-module infrastructure. RT-2 needs it when complete reducibility is proved and exploited; RT-1 does not.

contents.name: Proposition 1.2.4 equivalent characterizations of semisimplicity
contents.reason: The semisimplicity equivalences are exactly the next page's module-theoretic seam with MOD-4. They would overstate RT-1's scope if scaffolded here.

contents.name: Corollary 1.2.5 every finite-dimensional FG-module is semisimple when |G| is invertible
contents.reason: This is already a semisimplicity payoff of Maschke and depends on the MOD-4 semisimple-module interfaces. Keeping it here would collapse the RT-1/RT-2 seam the design deliberately separates.

contents.name: Corollary 1.2.6 the socle
contents.reason: Socle language is useful later in modular and projective representation theory, but it is not needed on this first page and the design does not allocate scope to it here.

contents.name: Corollary 1.2.7 uniqueness of isotypic components
contents.reason: Isotypic decomposition belongs after complete reducibility has been proved. The current page stops before that decomposition theory starts.

contents.name: Lemma 2.1.2 endomorphisms of the left regular module
contents.reason: The regular-module endomorphism computation is part of the Wedderburn route and is only needed once RT-2 starts decomposing the semisimple group algebra.

contents.name: Theorem 2.1.3 (Artin-Wedderburn)
contents.reason: Wedderburn's theorem is one of RT-2's landmark consequences. The current page prepares its hypotheses but does not build the matrix-product decomposition yet.

contents.name: Corollary 2.1.4 the complete set of simple modules and the dimension formula
contents.reason: This dimension count is part of the semisimple algebra package and feeds the later multiplicity and sum-of-squares results on RT-2.

contents.name: Corollary 2.1.5 the regular representation multiplicities and the sum-of-squares formula
contents.reason: The multiplicity formula and the sum of squares are Wedderburn consequences of semisimplicity. They belong on RT-2 with the actual decomposition of k[G], not before Maschke is even stated locally.

contents.name: Corollary 2.1.7 abelian groups over an algebraically closed field have degree 1
Proposition 4.2.1 degree 1 representations factor through G/G'
Example 4.2.2 the real 2-dimensional representation of C_3
Proposition 4.3.1 induction as a direct sum over cosets
contents.reason: This is one of the explicit induction models that the design assigns to RT-4. RT-1 only keeps the bare restriction interface and example-level permutation language.

contents.name: Proposition 4.3.2 the induced-module characterization by coset translates
contents.reason: The universal characterization of induction belongs with RT-4's Frobenius reciprocity package, not on the introductory group-ring page.

contents.name: 6.3 Radicals, socles and the augmentation ideal
Exercise 13 generators of the augmentation ideal
Exercise 15 kernels RG·I_N of quotient maps RG -> R[G/N]
contents.reason: This relative augmentation-ideal kernel is used for later modular and quotient-group structure results. The introductory RT-1 page only needs the absolute augmentation ideal and does not yet build quotient-group algebra machinery.

contents.name: Exercise 21 RG·I_H and the quotient RG/(RG·I_H)
contents.reason: This exercise is already written in induction language and belongs with the tensor-coset models of induction on RT-4. RT-1 keeps only the elementary restriction interface.

contents.name: Exercise 22 I_G/I_G^2 isomorphic to G/G'
contents.reason: The quotient I_G/I_G^2 is the first homological shadow of the augmentation ideal. It belongs to later group-cohomological or homological-algebra development, not to this first representation page.

contents.name: Theorem 9.2.6 finite-dimensional algebras have a splitting field of finite degree
contents.reason: Existence of a finite splitting extension is not needed to author the current page, whose statements are conditional on the chosen field and whose examples already name their base fields explicitly.

contents.name: Example 9.2.2 cyclic groups over nonsplitting fields

sources.title: Pavel Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory
sources.locator: Printed contents pp. 2-3; Chapter 1 §1.3, Proposition 1.16, and Corollaries 1.17-1.18, pp. 6-8; Chapter 3 §3.1, Proposition 3.2, Example 3.3, and the §3.3 examples on finite abelian groups and S_3, pp. 31-35.

contents.name: Proposition 1.16 Schur's lemma for irreducible representations
Corollary 1.17 Schur's lemma for algebraically closed fields
Corollary 1.18 commutative algebras have one-dimensional irreducibles
Theorem 3.1 (Maschke)
contents.reason: Etingof's chapter opens with Maschke because his page 3 already lives in semisimplicity and character theory. The commissioned RT-1 page stops before that threshold and hands it to RT-2.

contents.name: Proposition 3.2 the semisimplicity converse
contents.reason: The converse to Maschke is part of the same semisimplicity package as the Wedderburn decomposition of k[G], so it belongs on RT-2 with the characteristic-hypothesis discussion.

contents.name: Example 3.3 G = Z/pZ in characteristic p
contents.reason: This is again the standard characteristic-p failure of Maschke. The design explicitly reserves that witness for the next page rather than duplicating it here.
